item.title: New draft rules could dilute regulations for animal testing
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Activism, Animals, Environmental Law, Industry, Research, and Technology
item.description:
- Draft rules, open for public comment until November 5, would let institutional ethics committees approve “mild” and “moderate” experiments on animals which currently need central approval under prevailing regulations.
- Animal rights groups say the rules weaken protections, citing a conflict of interest in approvals and subjective severity categories.
- The draft rules also open the door to using wild and stray animals in experiments, as well as sourcing livestock from open markets.
item.content:encoded: The draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiment, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules, 2026 issued by the government on September 30, 2026 has drawn sharp criticism from animal rights groups across the country, including PETA, which said they could “significantly weaken existing animal protections.” The draft rules are open to public comments till November 5, 2026. The draft rules propose basing approvals for experiments on the expected severity of harm to the animal, departing from existing regulations — the Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules, 1968, and the Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules, 1998 — which take a more centralised approach to which animals can be used for experimentation. The draft rules allow institutional-level ethics committees to approve experiments of a “mild” and “moderate” nature, while deferring those of a “severe” nature or those from which the animal will not recover, to the central Committee for the Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA). Prevailing regulations require approvals from the CCSEA for any experiments on animals above the phylogenetic level of rodents and other small animals, such as birds and rabbits. “The draft rules list certain examples of experimentation — such as inducing tumours or solitary isolation — as being of a moderate nature. But these categorisations appear to be based on our perceptions of severity, and may not necessarily reflect whether it is mild, moderate, or severe on the animal per se,” says Surat Parvatam, Senior Program…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: When livelihoods adapt to a changing wetland
item.dc:creator: Debarun Choudhury
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Fishing, Floods, Lakes, Monsoons, Tourism, Water, Water Pollution, and Wetlands
item.description:
- Environmental changes such as siltation, pollution, overexploitation of resources, shrinking area and erratic rainfall events, impact Assam’s Son Beel wetland and the families that depend on it for livelihood.
- Farmers and fishers are adapting with integrated farming and seasonal fishing to diversify income opportunities.
- While the Assam government plans to develop tourism infrastructure and floating solar in Son Beel, the wetland is absent from its newly launched statewide restoration project.
item.content:encoded: Each year, as winter begins around mid November, Arup Das looks out across the marsh surrounding his home in Dargarbond, one of the many villages around Son Beel, a seasonal wetland in Assam. The land around him was submerged under water just a couple of months ago. Now, as the water recedes, he releases his ducks to forage for snails, aquatic plants, insects, and whatever else the retreating waters leave behind. Son Beel is the largest wetland in Assam with a fluctuating size since it expands during the monsoon and contracts during the dry season. More than 50,000 people depend directly on this wetland for their livelihoods. “A wetland is not simply a body of water,” says Tapati Das, an ecologist heading the Department of Ecology and Environmental Science at Assam University. “It is a system of inundation and retreat, of channels and marshes, which naturally replenishes a landscape in cycles.” Tapati describes Son Beel as a freshwater wetland with pronounced seasonal changes in water coverage. “During the monsoon, water spreads across the surrounding lowlands. Flooding expands aquatic habitat; recession concentrates organisms in remaining pools and exposes substrates for terrestrial plants and cultivation,” she elaborates. The seasonal shift is not a temporary interruption to Son Beel’s ecology. “It is part of how the wetland functions.” This cycle shapes fish habitats and determines when land will become available for crop cultivation, and also creates feeding grounds for Arup’s ducks. item.title: Study maps foot-and-mouth disease risk zones where livestock and wildlife overlap
item.dc:creator: Hirra Azmat
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Animals, Environment, Grazing, Health impacts, Human Wildlife Conflict, Migration, Protected Areas, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A new study in Jammu and Kashmir has mapped potential risk zones for the transmission of foot-and-mouth disease in areas where livestock migration routes overlap with areas with wildlife.
- While active FMD surveillance carried out by the animal husbandry department is focused on cattle, buffaloes, sheep, and goats, wildlife is not included in the surveillance.
- Protected areas (PAs) located closer to pastoral settlements face critical risk due to enhanced probability of interspecies contact, shared grazing grounds, and environmental contamination.
item.content:encoded: Every summer, Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoralists in Jammu and Kashmir move their livestock to the mountains in search of pastures. These routes bring the cattle closer to habitats of rare wild ungulates such as the endangered hangul (Kashmir red deer) and the markhor (wild goat). This is risky, as foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) outbreaks have been reported among livestock in the region with suspected FMD-like outbreaks occurring in July 2024 (in Kargil’s highland pastures) and May 2024 (in Bandipora and Pulwama districts). Widespread outbreaks were also recorded in 2021 across Budgam, Pulwama, and Srinagar. The pastoral routes could create opportunities for diseases such as FMD to spread from livestock to wildlife, although transmission in these areas has not been confirmed. A new study has mapped potential FMD risk zones in Jammu and Kashmir where livestock migration routes overlap with or lie close to protected areas. The study authors say that the findings can support veterinarians, conservationists, and policymakers in managing the deadly FMD transmission and aid in achieving One Health targets. Where livestock routes meet wildlife habitats Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral disease that affects cloven-hoofed animals, including cattle, buffaloes, sheep and goats. It is endemic among livestock in India, including Jammu and Kashmir. “While systematic mass vaccination under the National Animal Disease Control Programme (NADCP) by Animal Husbandry Department has helped dampen large-scale epidemics in Jammu and Kashmir, seasonal movement of Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoralists with their livestock and pockets of unvaccinated or partially immunised livestock continue…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: India’s emissions growth slows as renewable energy begins replacing coal, UNEP report finds
item.dc:creator: Manish Chandra Mishra
item.author: Shailesh Shrivastava
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Energy, Green Energy, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Renewable Energy, and United Nations
item.description:
- India’s greenhouse gas emissions broke from a longer period of rapid growth in 2025, according to UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026. However, different datasets disagree on whether emissions increased or declined slightly.
- Renewable electricity generation increased by 98 terawatt-hours in 2025, nearly twice the increase in electricity demand, while coal-fired generation declined by 44 terawatt-hours.
- Milder weather and slower electricity demand growth also contributed to the slowdown. Researchers caution that sustained emissions reductions will require greater investment in energy storage, transmission and industrial decarbonisation.
item.content:encoded: The upward trend of greenhouse gas emissions in India showed a significant change in 2025. The trend, which was indicating a longer period of rapid growth, has pivoted from this path and is now showing a slight decline in India’s emissions. This has been reported in the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) new report Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, released on October 21. The report finds that the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) and the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicate a slight decline in India’s emissions, while the Energy Institute estimates a marginal increase. However, all three indicate a departure from the country’s earlier pattern of rapid emissions growth, partly because of weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy. “The data this year is very encouraging,” said Minal Pathak, a researcher at Ahmedabad University and a lead author of the UNEP report’s chapter on global emissions trends, in a written response to Mongabay-India. She said the change was partly attributable to weather effects and structural shifts towards renewable energy, as highlighted in Chapter 2 of the report. India remains the world’s third-largest greenhouse gas emitter after China and the United States. Its emissions reached approximately 4.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2025, excluding land use and forestry. However, its per capita emissions of 3.1 tonnes were less than half the global average of 6.4 tonnes. item.title: Scientists explore whether Himalayan disasters can be anticipated
item.dc:creator: Max Martin
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Science, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, Global Warming, Himalayas, Impacts of Climate Change, Mountains, and Research
item.description:
- Satellite imagery shows some Himalayan slopes undergo measurable ground movements before catastrophic collapse.
- Remote sensing involves huge volumes of data, even for a target area, yet these warning signs were not enough to predict when the slope would finally collapse in the case of the recent Nepal disaster.
- Experts call for better localised forecasts and rigorous monitoring that can contribute to effective early warning and early action.
item.content:encoded: On October 11, 2026, a flash flood tore through Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki river basin in Gorkha district, hurling sediment and debris downstream, destroying homes and roads, and leaving many others homeless. The disaster struck less than seven weeks after a catastrophic collapse of rock and glacier ice on Langtang Lirung on August 26, which unleashed a destructive surge of ice and debris through the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor along the Nepal-China border. As Nepal tried to cope with the second disaster, a group of scientists was about to release a synthesis report. They reported that satellite signals indicated the mountain slope involved in the August Langtang Lirung collapse had moved measurably before it collapsed. Scientists are now exploring whether such satellite observations could be translated into reliable early warnings of catastrophic slope failures and save lives. The Budhi Gandaki river in Nepal. Image by Gaurav Dhwaj Khadka via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Clairvoyance from space ICIMOD scientists highlighted two sets of satellite observations in their synthesis report. The first, from Sentinel-1 radar, revealed that ground shifted by up to 40 cm along the satellite’s line of sight on the slopes of Langtang Lirung between July 7 and August 24, and that the slopes subsequently collapsed. Similarly, NISAR satellite radar recorded up to 30 cm of displacement in the same area between July 26 and August 19, they added. Both satellites use radar to detect changes in Earth’s surface and can see through clouds and darkness, which matters in the monsoon-bound Himalayas.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.content:encoded: A 19-month cheetah died from pellet wounds on October 27 at a veterinary facility in Jabalpur. The male cub was the offspring of Nirva, a South African cheetah brought to India under Project Cheetah, India’s effort to reintroduce the species decades after it was declared extinct in the country. Following the death of the cheetah, KNG22, the Union government has deputed a team comprising the Inspector General of Forests, National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), the Additional Director of the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) and the Regional Deputy Director of WCCB to investigate the incident on the ground. The Madhya Pradesh government has also constituted a Special Task Force (STF) with forest and police officers, to investigate the death. KNG22, born in India to six-year-old Nirva, was found injured on October 25 in the territorial forests of Morena, outside the protected area of Kuno National Park. The Madhya Pradesh Forest Department found the cheetah in Compartment No. 748 in the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division and provided intensive veterinary care and emergency surgery at the veterinary facility in Jabalpur. An initial X-ray and a subsequent CT scan at the Department of Veterinary Surgery and Radiology, NDVSU, Jabalpur, revealed multiple foreign bodies that had damaged the cheetah’s internal organs, musculoskeletal system and nervous system. During emergency surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from his body. “Despite the medical intervention, the cheetah succumbed to its injuries on 27 October 2026,” read a press note from Sameeta Rajora, Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Snow trout needs more than reintroduction to survive
item.dc:creator: Sameeksha Sharma
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Conservation, Extinction, Fish, Fishing, Himalayas, Impacts of Climate Change, Lakes, Mountains, and Wildlife
item.description:
- As part of a captive-breeding and release programme, 350 lab-bred snow trout fingerlings were released into Naini lake, Nainital, Uttarakhand, in April 2026. The species was considered locally extinct for thirty years. However, a significant number of the introduced fingerlings have died.
- While the exact cause has not been determined, experts point to Naini lake’s reduced oxygen levels and rising temperatures, driven by decades of pollution and accelerating climate change, as likely factors. Snow trout require water temperatures between 8°C and 22°C, while this summer, recorded temperatures rose up to 27°C.
- Experts suggest that the lake environment must be restored before reintroducing snow trout to achieve conservation success.
item.content:encoded: On April 27, 2026, scientists from Kumaun University’s Department of Zoology released the first batch of snow trout fingerlings into a cage in Naini lake, Nainital, Uttarakhand. The fingerlings were part of a captive-breeding programme to revive the snow trout (Schizothorax richardsonii). Locally called Asela, the native cold-water Himalayan fish has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2010. Considered locally extinct for thirty years, its populations have declined steeply in other lakes of the region. Using Biofloc and recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) technology, scientists lab-bred the fish over two phases before releasing roughly 350 fingerlings into a cage in Naini lake. In June, the initiative expanded to the three other lakes, Bhimtal, Sattal and Naukuchiatal, with smaller cages. However, more than half of the fingerlings died in Naini lake, with similar reports from Bhimtal and other lakes, report the programme staff. The causes remain unknown, but the high mortality raises a larger question: can a reintroduction programme sustain fish in the very lakes that pushed them towards extinction through pollution, habitat destruction and climate change impacts? A dead snow trout fingerling retrieved from the Kumaon University experimental cage installed in Bhimtal Lake on June 24. Image by Sameeksha Sharma. A lake on life support Snow trout once thrived across Kumaon lakes through the 1980s before their populations collapsed due to sewage pollution, dropping oxygen levels and increased competition with exotic species such as the common carp. item.title: Citizens push back infrastructure projects that threaten green cover
item.dc:creator: Sohel Sarkar
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Activism, Cities and Towns, Ecology, Ecosystem services, Plants, and Trees
item.description:
- Bengaluru residents are protesting the loss of trees to elevated corridors and tunnel roads, with some of them counting trees at risk and questioning official estimates of tree loss.
- While mature trees and connected green spaces are vital safeguards against urban heat, studies show Bengaluru has lost 88% of its vegetation cover in five decades.
- Ecologists warn that compensatory planting and tree transplantation projected as remedies cannot fully offset tree loss.
item.content:encoded: Bengaluru, a city rapidly losing its green cover to infrastructure projects, had an important job to do: count its trees. In August 2019, the Karnataka High Court mandated the exercise under the Karnataka Preservation of Trees Act, 1976, setting a three-year deadline which wasn’t completed even seven years later. Residents in some neighbourhoods decided to then take the task into their own hands, driven by the apprehension of losing trees to several large-scale infrastructure projects announced for the city, including flyovers and tunnel roads. What they found has prompted them to push back against some of these impending projects. In east Bengaluru’s Indiranagar, a group of residents mapped the trees along the alignment of a proposed 13-km flyover from Swami Vivekananda Metro Station in the east to Silk Board Junction in the south, via Indiranagar. The flyover’s detailed project report (DPR) estimates that 89 trees will be felled for the proposed elevated corridor, while 235 trees fall within its construction width. The latter figure indicates the number of trees within the designated construction area, not necessarily the number that will be cut. Unconvinced that these figures reflected the trees on the ground, I Change Indiranagar, a network of resident welfare associations in the area, decided to conduct an independent survey, starting with a roughly 3.5-km stretch of the route. The group counted 1,001 trees. There is, however, a caveat. The DPR’s count of 235 trees covers the entire 13-km flyover alignment, while the residents surveyed only one section of it.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Chromium in water upends life in an industrial neighbourhood
item.dc:creator: Esha Lohia
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Groundwater, Health impacts, Human Rights, Industry, Water, and Water Pollution
item.description:
- Toxic chromium in borewell water has left hundreds of Nashik residents with painful skin conditions.
- Safe water is still irregular, and families pay for treatment and clean water while facing stigma.
- Activists warn the pollution may reach the Godavari, as a promised effluent treatment plant remains unbuilt.
item.content:encoded: For the past two months, 55-year-old Gangubai Laxmigan Shivale has been feeding her family on food bought from outside. “There is constant itching, and blood pours out if I scratch the rashes on my hand, so I can’t cook,” says Shivale, a resident of Dattanagar, a residential area next to the Ambad industrial estate on the outskirts of Nashik city in Maharashtra. “We are a family of four, and we all sustain on samosas, vada pav and other food from outside.” She is one of around 400 residents of Dattanagar who have reported severe rashes, chemical ulcers, swollen lymph nodes, black lesions and other skin problems, which they attribute to contaminated groundwater. When residents draw water from their borewells, it runs bright yellow into their buckets. A laboratory test of water from a borewell adjoining stream of Nandini river near the city’s Ambad industrial area validated their concern. It found chromium at more than 1,000 times the permissible limit for drinking water. The test was commissioned by the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People (SANDRP), a non-governmental organisation and carried out by Ashwamedh Engineers and Consultants, an independent laboratory. The sample showed total chromium of 50.5 milligrams per litre (mg/L), of which 50.3 mg/L was hexavalent chromium. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) allows only 0.05 mg/L of chromium in drinking water. item.title: Winged wayfarers of the ocean
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Animals, Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Oceans, and Wildlife
item.description: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. With their flattened bodies and wing-like fins, rays are a striking sight when they glide in ocean waters. But many rays face an uncertain future: a recent study found that most Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) in Indian waters along the Bay of Bengal […]
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. With their flattened bodies and wing-like fins, rays are a striking sight when they glide in ocean waters. But many rays face an uncertain future: a recent study found that most Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) in Indian waters along the Bay of Bengal fall outside marine protected areas, leaving critical breeding and nursery habitats vulnerable. Rays are cartilaginous fish closely related to sharks. Found worldwide, they are mostly marine, though a few species live in freshwater lakes and rivers. Most ray species are benthic (dwelling on the ocean floor), while a few live in the open ocean. Depending on the species, they feed on zooplankton, krill, fish, molluscs, worms, crustaceans, and marine mammals, thereby shaping seabed communities and cycling nutrients. There are diverse groups of rays, ranging from manta rays (the largest type, with some growing as wide as a minibus) to stingrays, which have whip-like venomous tails. Nearly all rays have flattened, disc-shaped bodies with wing-like pectoral fins. A unique lineage is the rhino rays (order Rhinopristiformes), which have flattened, ray-like bodies but shark-like tails and pointed snouts. These comprise 68 species of saw-fishes, wedgefishes, giant guitar-fishes, guitarfishes and banjo rays. According to the IUCN Red List, rhino rays are the world’s most threatened marine fish, with over 70% of assessed species considered threatened, and nearly half critically endangered. item.title: Centre says tribal leaders are not ‘necessary’ parties to Great Nicobar forest rights dispute
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Forest Rights Act, Forests, Indigenous Peoples, Indigenous Rights, Islands, Land Rights, and Tribes
item.description:
- The Union Tribal Affairs Ministry has told the Calcutta High Court that Nicobarese leaders seeking to join a petition on Great Nicobar forest rights are “neither necessary nor proper parties,” and were “sleeping over” their rights during the statutory process.
- The Nicobarese petitioners allege that the 2022 forest rights settlement enabling the Island’s mega development project relied on consent from non-tribal settlers.
- Though the government maintains forest rights are settled, its own annual report shows zero claims settled in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
item.content:encoded: The Union Tribal Affairs Ministry has said that Nicobarese leaders seeking to join a petition challenging the settlement of forest rights on Great Nicobar Island are “neither necessary nor proper parties,” in the case, court documents show. The Nicobarese are one of two major tribes affected by the development of the Island, and primary claimants to forest rights in the area. An ongoing petition in the Calcutta High Court, filed by former IAS officer Meena Gupta, has challenged the Union government’s claim that rights under the Forest Rights Act (2005) (FRA) were settled on the Island. The FRA recognises the historical rights of tribal and other forest dwelling communities over forest resources, and makes compliance with its statutes necessary in clearing forest land for diversion. On July 9, 2026, four Nicobarese residents sought to join Gupta’s plea, arguing that government certifications claiming the settlement of forest rights was based on gram sabha consent from non-tribal settler communities. Apart from the Nicobarese and Shompen — a particularly vulnerable and largely uncontacted tribe — the Island is inhabited by families of ex-servicemen from the mainland who were settled on the remote Island from 1969 onwards as part of a state-sponsored scheme. “This certificate falsely states that the concerned Gram Sabhas have consented to the diversion of forest lands and cites meetings of the Gram Sabhas of the settler community in which no Nicobarese were present,” the impleadment document submitted to the court, seen by Mongabay-India, says. “No Gram Sabha meeting of the…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Farmers prepare for low rain but get floods instead
item.dc:creator: Sameeksha Sharma
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Extreme Weather Events, Food, Impacts of Climate Change, Monsoons, and Villages
item.description:
- Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh received 90% more rainfall than normal during the 2026 monsoon, flooding fields after farmers had prepared for a drier season based on forecasts of a strong El Niño.
- Tenant and small farmers face additional hurdles in accessing compensation, with land ownership, documentation and delayed claim processing affecting their access to insurance support.
- The widening gap between seasonal forecasts and localised weather events, makes it harder for farmers to plan according to the crop calendar.
item.content:encoded: “At the Krishi Vigyan Kendra in July, we were told to plant more sesame, groundnut and urad. These are crops expected to withstand less rain. But God decided to flood our fields instead,” shares Jaidevi, a farmer in Chandpura, a village in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, pointing to her withered sesame crop. Jaidevi and her husband own three bighas of farmland and have struggled to make a living from it. Chandpura is among the worst hit villages by intense rainfall in Mahoba during this southwest monsoon. Ahead of the 2026 southwest monsoon, Mahoba’s Krishi Vigyan Kendra advised farmers to sow low-water crops, anticipating low rainfall because of the effects of El Niño this year. The monsoon arrived nearly 20 days late, with deficient rainfall for much of the season that typically starts mid-June. But the pattern reversed in late August, when heavy rain lashed the region, leaving much of farmland waterlogged by September 15. This year’s El Niño forecast is expected to be one of the strongest on record. Its impact in India is in the form of a weaker monsoon and warmer temperatures. In June, the agriculture ministry classified Mahoba as one of 111 high-priority districts based on irrigation coverage and vulnerability to rainfall deficits. Irrigation coverage in these districts is expected to be below 25 percent. Part of the drought-prone Bundelkhand region, Mahoba has long faced rainfall deficits, falling groundwater levels and limited irrigation. item.title: UN Loss and Damage Fund provisionally approves $21.6 million for flood-hit Nepal
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Global Warming, and Impacts of Climate Change
item.description: Nepal, which suffered a catastrophic debris flow and flash flood on August 26, is slated to receive $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The decision to “provisionally” release the funds was finalised during an “extraordinary meeting” convened by the Fund’s board on October 22. Nepal will still […]
item.content:encoded: Nepal, which suffered a catastrophic debris flow and flash flood on August 26, is slated to receive $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The decision to “provisionally” release the funds was finalised during an “extraordinary meeting” convened by the Fund’s board on October 22. Nepal will still need to apply for this funding, and the Board will consider the request at its next meeting, the tenth FRLD Board meeting, this December. “Following Nepal’s formal letter on August 31, 2026 requesting support from the Fund, the FRLD Board commenced to assess available options. Backed by strong solidarity from the whole Board, intensive consultations were held throughout September and October, culminating in today’s extraordinary Board meeting, in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure,” an FRLD press statement said. The FRLD was constituted in 2023 with the specific purpose of providing rapid financial support to developing countries struggling with the economic and non-economic losses and damages associated with climate-driven extreme weather events. The demand by developing countries for a funding facility for losses and damages had been simmering at the climate Conference of Parties (COP) meetings for decades. The decision to provisionally release funding to Nepal comes ahead of the COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled to take place from November 9 to November 20. Climate change was “a destabilising factor” in the Nepal flash flood, according to a report by the World Weather Attribution. item.title: The Sundarbans at the crossroads of climate change and human survival [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: C.P. Rajendran
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.locations: Bay of Bengal, Global, and West Bengal
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Biodiversity, Climate Change, Ecology, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Forests, Global Warming, Impacts of Climate Change, Mangroves, Rivers, Salinisation, Sea Level Rise, Villages, Wetlands, and Wildlife
item.description:
- The Indian Sundarbans has become a major source of climate-induced displacement and distress migration in India.
- The Amphibious Living Opportunities approach offers a path forward by combining resilient housing, diversified climate-adapted livelihoods, and community-driven initiatives.
- The framework’s success will depend on sustained investment, institutional commitment, and the active participation of the communities most at risk.
- The views in this commentary are those of the author.
item.content:encoded: Spanning India and Bangladesh, with India comprising 40% of its area, a vast and ever-shifting mangrove forest stretches across the Bay of Bengal. This vast delta derives its name from the Sundari (Heritiera fomes), the tall mangrove species that flourishes here in abundance. The name “Sundarbans” is a modern rendering of “Sunderbunds,” a term coined by Walter Hamilton in the East India Gazetteer, meaning “Forests of the Soondry” (“Sundri,” or beautiful). Heritiera fomes is the abundant tall mangrove species of the region. Where the rivers Ganga (Padma in Bangladesh), Brahmaputra, and Meghna discharge into the Bay of Bengal, they form the Sundarbans — the largest contiguous mangrove forest on Earth. Toward the coast, the forest transitions into a low-lying swamp of sand dunes, mud flats, and barren expanses, intersected by innumerable tidal streams and channels. Four protected areas within this remarkable landscape are recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Sundarbans West, South, and East in Bangladesh, and Sundarbans National Park in India. The nutrient-rich mangrove waters of India’s eastern coast form a vital breeding ground and nursery for roughly 90% of the region’s aquatic species. The ecosystem is notable for supporting overlapping populations of threatened aquatic mammals, including the Ganges river dolphin and the Irrawaddy dolphin. This extraordinary species concentration in the Sundarbans stems from the dynamic mixing of freshwater from major rivers — the Ganga and the Brahmaputra among them — with the saltwater of the Bay of Bengal. item.title: Community models could help conserve the disappearing migratory freshwater fish [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Dewan
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Extinction, Fish, Himalayas, Mountains, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Migratory freshwater fish have declined by 81% globally since the 1970s, with the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin as a critical migration landscape where river giants like the golden mahseer are quietly disappearing.
- As riverbed habitats are disappearing with the impacts of climate change, impassable hydropower dams like Tehri and Srinagar are trapping fish into small, inbred, genetic islands.
- Decentralised, local stewardship can successfully restore wild fish populations while sustaining river livelihoods.
- The views in the commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: When the United Nations Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) published its Global Assessment of Migratory Freshwater Fishes report earlier this year, the numbers confirmed what riverine communities had suspected for decades. Migratory freshwater fish populations have dropped 81% globally since the 1970s. Nearly all (97%) of the 58 fish species listed under the convention now face extinction. The report, drafted in collaboration with the UN Environment Programme-World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) names the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) river system as a global priority region. Zeb Hogan, a fish biologist and one of the report’s lead authors, describes the GBM basin as among South Asia’s greatest migration landscapes. It is a single connected pathway from Himalayan headwaters down to the Bay of Bengal. Yet, despite supporting an immense biomass of migratory species, the basin is collapsing under severe habitat fragmentation driven by aggressive hydropower expansion and altered flow regimes. Public debate about the GBM usually stops at the lower reaches, majorly at barrages like Farakka. The damage is worse far above the plains. In the high-altitude headwaters of the Indian Himalayan Region, the lifelines that flow-dependent species depend on are being cut apart piece by piece. Cascading hazards and the dislocation of aquatic life In late August 2026, a massive ice and rock avalanche struck the Nepal-Tibet border. The debris tore into the Lende Khola before surging down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. item.title: Cloud seeding’s potential to ease drought is uncertain
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Sreekandan
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Science, Drought, Extreme Weather Events, and Water
item.description:
- Karnataka recorded a 35% rainfall deficit between June 1 and September 30, 2026.
- The government launched a 60-day cloud-seeding programme to address the state’s rainfall deficit, despite warnings of unfavourable conditions.
- Weather experts have called for caution, noting that there may be too few rain-bearing clouds to seed. They also raise concerns about limited public communication on this effort.
item.content:encoded: The Karnataka government launched a cloud-seeding programme in September to address rainfall deficits in drought-affected parts of the state. Since the launch of the programme, worth around ₹28 crore (₹285 million), questions have been raised about the viability of cloud-seeding operations this late in the monsoon. Cloud seeding is a disputed weather modification technique that introduces particles into suitable existing clouds to influence how precipitation forms. It cannot create new clouds, and its effect on rainfall is difficult to measure. Weather experts, including senior IMD officials, have cautioned that “conditions are not favourable” for cloud seeding in Karnataka. Highest rainfall deficit on record “For the people of Karnataka, drought is a very common feature,” says G.S. Srinivasa Reddy, former director of the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC), who has 35 years of experience in real-time weather monitoring. Since the turn of the 21st century, Reddy says, 17 of the 26 years have been drought years in Karnataka. But 2026 has been particularly severe, as the state recorded just 551 millimetres of rainfall between June 1 and September 30, a record 35% rainfall deficit. According to the KSNDMC, 30 districts and 209 taluks in the state recorded rainfall ranging from “deficit” to “large deficit” in the June to September period. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast notes that 2026 will be an El Niño year, and, according to Reddy, almost 60% of Karnataka’s drought years have coincided with El Niño. item.title: The toxic tyre chemical no one is measuring
item.dc:creator: Lakshmi Nilakantan
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Environment, Fish, Industry, Pollution, Rivers, Roads, and Water Pollution
item.description:
- A chemical used to make tyres last longer turns into 6PPD-quinone, a toxin linked to mass deaths of salmon in the U.S.
- With vehicle and tyre sales rising in India, experts warn the problem could grow, but no data exists on the toxin’s levels in Indian road dust, stormwater or water bodies.
- Experts call for regulating 6PPD and better stormwater management, as poor drainage and sewage-laden storm drains in Indian cities could carry the toxin into water bodies.
item.content:encoded: Every time a vehicle moves, its tyres shed tiny particles. Some of these particles carry a chemical that, in the U.S., was found killing salmon in urban streams after rain. India is selling more vehicles than ever before, yet experts say there is no data on how much of this chemical reaches the country’s rivers. The chemical is 6PPD (N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine), an additive used worldwide to increase tyre durability. It became a concern after researchers from the U.S. published a study in the journal Science in December 2020, linking a compound formed from 6PPD to mass deaths of coho salmon in urban streams after rain. “6PPD is used to neutralise ozone, prevent cracks in the rubber, and extend the lifespan of the tyre,” according to a January review article in RSC Advances by the Royal Society of Chemistry. The review opens by noting that India’s tyre market is expanding with its automotive industry, then examines the toxic effects of 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a byproduct formed when 6PPD reacts with ozone. Echoing the same, Paul Sharp, a chemist and Professor Emeritus, University of Missouri, Columbia, USA, says, “6PPD-Q is the ozonisation byproduct of 6PPD and formed as a tyre wear particle. It has no boundaries and is ubiquitous all over the motorised world. These can make their way into water bodies during rainstorms, leading to rapid/mass death of aquatic species.” Responding to Mongabay-India’s email interview, Sharp explains that as tyres wear down, 6PPD reacts with ground-level ozone to form 6PPD-Q. item.title: How Columbus’ voyages accelerated the homogenisation of Earth’s biodiversity [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: R.J. Ranjit Daniels
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Animals, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, and Extinction
item.description:
- Columbus’ arrival in the New World ushered in global biogeographical shifts and ecological disruption, weakening the resilience of the biosphere.
- His voyages set in motion an unprecedented exchange of biodiversity across geographical boundaries.
- Introduced microorganisms, plants and animals spread to new regions, with some becoming invasive or causing epidemics, contributing to biogeographical homogenisation.
- The views in this commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: Christopher Columbus was a legendary 15th-century Italian explorer whose “misadventures” opened the way for large-scale biogeographical homogenisation. Over the past 500 years, since Columbus first sailed west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach the “New World”, Earth has witnessed unprecedented cross-boundary human movement and the exchange of living organisms. These movements have brought about major shifts in the geographical distribution of microorganisms, plants and animals. While thousands of introduced plants and animals have acquired the deplorable status of “invasive alien species”, introduced pathogenic microorganisms, such as those that cause smallpox, cholera, sexually transmitted diseases and plague, have been major culprits in wiping out indigenous human populations and cultures across the world. History has also shown that introduced phytopathogenic microorganisms have devastated agriculture, causing widespread famine and human suffering. The post-Columbus transformation of Earth’s biogeography has proved catastrophic. In 1995, when UNESCO celebrated the silver jubilee of its Man and the Biosphere Programme, the event was held in Seville, Spain, where Columbus was laid to rest. The choice of venue could have hinted at Columbus’ unintentional contribution to the ecological chaos that Earth has witnessed over the past 500 years. Biogeographical periods shaping the biosphere Biogeography is the science that seeks to understand the patterns of geographical distribution of organisms and the reasons behind them, as well as the ecosystems in which organisms develop and coexist. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, […]
item.content:encoded: New research from the Centre for Wildlife Studies evaluated changing fire regimes in wildlife reserves across three Indian landscapes, finding that burned area rose most steeply in the Eastern Ghats between 2002 and 2022, at 9.3% per year. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, climate, and repeated human ignition than the Western Ghats, while Central India sits in between. The study evaluated roughly 20,000 square kilometres of protected forest land across 13 reserves. Both human and climate factors explained between 21 and 77% of annual fire activity across individual reserves, with drought and community fire use both playing major, but regionally varying roles. A region- and reserve-specific deconstruction of forest fires is essential to understanding how different rainfall, temperature, and land use regimes, as well as population densities, affect fire occurrence, the researchers argue. For example, high human population density was strongly associated with more frequent fires in Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary (Telangana) and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (Andhra Pradesh), but in Nagarahole and Bandipur National Parks (Karnataka), similar conditions were linked with fewer fires. “Various factors could be contributing to this paradoxical trend in burned areas in India, including forest management, land-use change, changes in fire ignitions, anthropogenic climate change and natural climate variability,” the study says. Using satellite-derived burned-area data from NASA’s MODIS sensor, the study found that burned area in the Western Ghats declined by 10.8% per year. item.title: The endurance runner of the grasslands
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Grasslands, Mammals, and Wildlife
item.description: A creature of the open grasslands, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast.
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. A creature of the open grasslands, where there’s nowhere to hide, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast, sometimes even fast enough to have once outrun the Asiatic cheetah when it still prevailed in India. The blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra) is the sole living member of its genus. In a 2025 story published in Mongabay-India, Mihir Godbole, founder of The Grasslands Trust-India, said: “Blackbucks … are key indicators that grassland species cannot do well in any other habitats.” Female blackbucks are light brown and live in herds, sometimes led by a mature male. Younger males live in bachelor groups until they mature, at which point they establish their own territories, develop a black-brown coat, and grow corkscrewed horns. During mating season, males form display territories called leks, leaping and calling to attract females. Once spread across the Indian subcontinent, blackbuck populations were decimated by trophy hunting under British rule. The species is now extinct in the wild in Pakistan and Bangladesh and survives in small protected pockets in Nepal, while the majority live in India. A 2016 estimate put the Indian population at roughly 35,000. They live in the open grassland habitats and are found across 13 states, with strongholds in Velavadar, Tal Chhapar, Point Calimere, and Karnataka’s Ranebennur and Jayamangali reserves.
